title: Sparks and Lightning
description: Charge, current and voltage, static sparks, the Leyden jar and what lightning really is
tryIt: On a dry day, rub a balloon on a wool jumper and see how many torn paper scraps it lifts, then try again in a steamy bathroom.

concepts.title: How it works: charge, sparks and a jar
concepts.contentHtml:
The grid is down, the house is dark and silent, and when you pull off your wool jumper in the gloom it crackles with tiny blue sparks. That crackle is this whole skill in miniature. Before you can make electricity, you need to know what it is.

Everything is built of atoms, and atoms hold protons (positive) and electrons (negative) in balance. Electrons can be moved. When you comb your hair, electrons leave the atoms and molecules in your hair and travel to the plastic comb, so the comb ends up negatively charged and your hair positive. Opposite charges attract and like charges repel, which is why combed hair stands on end. Shocks come from gaining or losing electric charge in a hurry.

People had noticed electrical forces for more than a thousand years, but the English physician William Gilbert, in De Magnete (1600), gave us much of the vocabulary, including the word electricity. Storing it came next. Around 1745, Ewald von Kleist in Pomerania and Pieter van Musschenbroek in Leyden made what became known as the Leyden jar: at its simplest, a glass bottle partly filled with water with a wire running into it. Later jars swapped the water for metal foil lining the inside and outside of the glass.

Musschenbroek charged his jar, touched the wire and felt his whole body shaken “as by a lightning stroke”; he wrote that he “believed that I was done for”. Linked jars stored more, and Benjamin Franklin called a row of them a battery, but unlike a real battery Leyden jars released all their energy in a single burst. They never went away: miniaturised, they are hard at work today under a new name, the capacitor.

concepts.title: In the field: your first circuit
concepts.contentHtml:
Static is spectacular but useless: it arrives in one crack and is gone. Useful electricity flows steadily round a loop, and three words describe it. Current is the rate of charge flow past a point, measured in amperes: one amp is one coulomb of charge per second. Voltage is the push, the electric potential energy per unit charge, measured in volts. Resistance, in ohms, is how hard the path fights back. For many conductors the current is directly proportional to the voltage applied, which is Ohm's law: amps equal volts divided by ohms.

  1. Make a loop. Electricity travels in closed circuits. A break anywhere stops the flow everywhere.
  2. Pick a tiny source. One or two torch cells, or the lemon battery from the next lesson. Nothing bigger.
  3. Add a resistor. A bare shop battery is too powerful for a small LED and will wreck it; a resistor in the loop slows the current.
  4. Mind the LED's direction. An LED only lights if it is connected the right way round. Dark? Turn it over.
  5. Add a switch. A switch is just a gap you can open and close on purpose.
  6. Draw it first. Sketch the loop with symbols before you touch a wire, and check every part sits in one unbroken ring.
Safety Stay with cells of a few volts. Never open, touch or wire into sockets or house wiring: the HSE warns that normal mains voltage, 230 volts AC, can kill. Never join a battery's terminals with bare wire or a metal tool, because the short circuit sends a large current through the metal and makes it very hot very quickly. And if you hear thunder, go indoors: if you can hear it, you are already in danger of being struck.

concepts.title: Myth check: lightning and Franklin's kite
concepts.contentHtml:
Lightning is your jumper's crackle scaled up to the size of a storm. Inside a thundercloud, collisions between ice and hail charge the particles: the lighter ice crystals become positively charged and are carried upward, while the heavier hail turns negative. The middle of the cloud ends up negative and pulls the ground beneath it positive. Air insulates until the difference grows too great, then breaks down in a giant spark that can heat the air to 50,000 °F, about five times hotter than the surface of the Sun. The air expands so fast that it booms: count the seconds from flash to bang and divide by five for the distance in miles (by three, roughly, for kilometres).

Myth Franklin's kite was struck by lightning, and he caught the bolt in a jar.
Reality According to the Franklin Institute, the kite was not struck by lightning, and if it had been, he probably would have been electrocuted. It picked up the charge already in the stormy air over Philadelphia in June 1752: loose threads of the wet hemp string stood on end, a spark jumped from the key to his knuckle, and he charged a Leyden jar from it. He was not even first: Thomas-François Dalibard had shown the electrical nature of lightning in France a month earlier, and a year after Franklin, Georg Wilhelm Richmann was killed by ball lightning while trying a similar experiment.
Myth Lightning never strikes the same place twice.
Reality It often strikes the same place repeatedly, especially tall, pointed, isolated objects: the Empire State Building is hit an average of 23 times a year.

Wait, really? Static is not made by friction at all. It is the mere contact between two different materials that moves the charge; rubbing just brings more surface into contact. Damp air is the enemy, which is why static tricks flop on a humid day.

title: Cells from Lemons and Metal
description: Galvani's frogs, Volta's pile, fruit batteries, why two metals make a voltage, and the Baghdad battery
tryIt: Push a copper strip and a galvanised nail into each of four lemons, wire them copper to zinc in a chain, and see if they light a small red LED.

concepts.title: How it works: frogs, metals and Volta's pile
concepts.contentHtml:
Your torch batteries are dead and the nearest shop is a burnt-out shell. In the rubble you find a sheet of zinc-coated roofing, a coil of copper wire and a sack of lemons. Two centuries ago, that haul would have put you at the cutting edge of science.

It began with frogs. In 1786 Luigi Galvani, a doctor at the University of Bologna, made a frog's muscle twitch by touching its nerves with a pair of scissors during an electrical storm, and he explained it as animal electricity. Alessandro Volta, a physics professor at Pavia, disagreed. He argued that the frog's legs were only a detector and that the contact of dissimilar metals was the true source.

To prove it he needed a steady source with no animal in it. In March 1800 he wrote to Sir Joseph Banks, president of the Royal Society of London, describing a column of silver and zinc plates with a moistened disc between each pair, built “as high as possible without any danger of its falling”. He tried many metals; zinc with copper became the classic pair, separated by pasteboard or cloth dampened with brine or vinegar. Each sandwich of two metals and a wet layer is one cell, and the voltages of the cells add up: the higher the stack, the harder the push. His first piles probably gave around 0.75 volts per cell.

Unlike a Leyden jar, the pile needed no charging and gave a steady current. Within months William Nicholson and Anthony Carlisle used one to split water into hydrogen and oxygen, and Humphry Davy later built a pile of 2,000 elements and discovered several alkali metals with it, sodium and potassium among them. The unit of electrical push, the volt, is named in Volta's honour.

concepts.title: In the field: a fruit battery
concepts.contentHtml:
A lemon battery is Volta's pile with the wet cloth swapped for fruit. The citric acid of the lemon reacts with the zinc and loosens electrons, and copper pulls electrons more strongly than zinc, so when you join the two metals with a wire, electrons flow from the zinc to the copper as a current. The zinc is slowly eaten away as it gives up its electrons. Two strips of the same metal give nothing: you need two metals with different electrical potentials and a liquid that carries ions between them.

  1. Wake the juice. Roll the lemon firmly on a table to release the juice inside.
  2. Two different metals. Push in a copper strip and, a little way off, a galvanised nail: it works because it is coated with zinc.
  3. Measure. If you have a voltmeter, one lemon will probably read less than 1 volt, while a small LED needs about 2.
  4. Chain them. Join three or four lemons in series, copper of one to zinc of the next, so their voltages add.
  5. Connect the LED. Wire the free zinc and free copper ends to its legs. Still dark? Swap the legs over.
  6. Experiment. Try oranges, apples or other pairs of metals, and see which gives the highest voltage.
Safety This is about the safest electricity there is, but treat the fruit as scrap afterwards and do not eat it. Never cut open shop batteries to borrow their zinc: battery electrolytes can contain very corrosive chemicals that can permanently damage the eyes and burn the skin. And do not test your LED straight on a shop battery, which will simply destroy it.

concepts.title: Myth check: lemon power and the Baghdad battery
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth The lemon is the fuel.
Reality The lemon is only the wet layer. The energy comes from the metals, above all the zinc that dissolves; the juice just carries ions. Volta himself noticed that salt water worked better than pure water in his moistened discs, and he never needed fruit at all.

A more famous fruit-free cell comes from Iraq. In 1938 the German archaeologist Wilhelm König, working at Khujut Rabu just outside Baghdad, described a clay jar about 13 cm long holding a copper cylinder that encased an iron rod, and he decided it was a battery. Fill a replica with vinegar or grape juice and it does work: replicas made by students under the historian Marjorie Senechal produced from 0.8 to nearly two volts.

Myth The Baghdad battery proves the ancients had electricity.
Reality Working is not the same as being used. No wires have ever been found, and even the British Museum metallurgist Paul Craddock, who thought the jars were batteries, admitted that without them “our interpretation of them could be completely wrong”. A claim that replicas electroplated silver in a German museum in 1978 was never written up; the experiments weren't even documented by photos. Similar vessels from nearby Seleucia are thought to have held scrolls, and in 2012 Elizabeth Stone, an expert on Iraqi archaeology, said not one archaeologist she knew believed the jars were batteries. The original was looted in 2003.

Wait, really? Experts have not always agreed: a 2003 BBC report said most archaeologists then accepted the devices as batteries, the opposite of Stone's view. And there is a physics catch. Stacking cells adds volts, but a weak cell pushes only a feeble current, and even the BBC noted that current is the real limiting factor for what tens of these jars could ever have done.

title: Magnets into Motion
description: Ørsted's twitching compass, Faraday's ring and coil, and how a dynamo turns motion into current
tryIt: Lay a compass under a length of wire, touch the wire's ends to an AA battery for a second or two, and watch the needle swing as Ørsted's did.

concepts.title: How it works: Ørsted's needle and Faraday's ring
concepts.contentHtml:
Your lemon chain can just about make an LED glow, and the lemons are going mouldy. What you want is a machine: something a stream or your own arm can turn, that pushes out current for as long as it keeps turning. The road to it began with a compass that moved when it should not have.

One April evening in 1820, getting ready to lecture at the University of Copenhagen, Hans Christian Ørsted noticed that whenever he connected or disconnected his circuit to a voltaic pile, a compass needle near the wire moved. Electricity and magnetism were linked. An Italian, Gian Domenico Romagnosi, had seen the same thing 18 years earlier, but his newspaper report made little impact. Within a week of hearing Ørsted's news, André-Marie Ampère began writing the theory.

In London the self-taught Michael Faraday went further. In 1821 he made a wire circle round a magnet in a bath of mercury, the first electric motor; his 1822 version still survives at the Royal Institution. If current could make motion, could magnetism make current? He succeeded on 29 August 1831 with an iron ring wound with two separate coils, insulated with cotton, a job that probably took about ten working days. Sending current through one coil made a brief current in the other.

His published account shows how odd it looked. The meter needle jumped, “but though the contact was continued, the effect was not permanent”; when he broke the circuit it swung again “in the contrary direction”. That autumn he pushed a bar magnet into a coil: “the magnet was suddenly thrust in; immediately the needle was deflected”. The rule is electromagnetic induction: any change in the magnetic field through a coil makes a voltage in it, whether you move the magnet, move the coil or switch an electromagnet on and off. No change, no current.

concepts.title: In the field: a shake-and-spin generator
concepts.contentHtml:
You can rebuild Faraday's discovery from scrap. The Exploratorium science museum in San Francisco publishes a design called the Stripped-Down Generator: a plastic tube with a stack of magnets sliding inside and a coil of fine wire round its middle. Whenever a wire and a magnetic field move across each other, a voltage is induced, and a coil multiplies it: the voltage obtained is the single-wire voltage multiplied by the number of turns.

  1. Make the tube. Roll two clear plastic sheets into a tube and plug each end; the design uses plastic film canisters.
  2. Wind the coil. Wrap about 60 metres of thin lacquered magnet wire round the middle, about 500 turns, tight but without squashing the tube.
  3. Bare the ends. Scrape the lacquer off the last few centimetres of each end so the copper makes contact, and clip them to an LED's legs.
  4. Load the magnets. Slide in a stack of ring magnets (the design uses five ceramic “donut” magnets) and cap the tube.
  5. Shake hard. Each time the magnets pass through the coil the LED should flash. It shows best in a dark room.
  6. Go round and round. A magnet spinning beside a coil does the same job without the shaking: that is a dynamo.

Faraday built a round-and-round version himself, a copper disc spinning between the poles of a magnet, and called it “a new electrical machine”. The pulses from a moving magnet flow one way and then the other, which is alternating current, and the generators that power your home work on the same general principle. Virtually all electric power is produced using Faraday's principles, whatever turns the generator.

Safety Keep home-made generators at LED-and-battery scale and never connect one to sockets or house wiring: normal mains voltage, 230 volts AC, can kill. For Ørsted's compass trick, touch the wire to the battery for a second or two only. A wire left across the terminals is a short circuit, and a large current makes the metal very hot very quickly.

concepts.title: Myth check: free power and Faraday's tax joke
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth A dynamo makes electricity for free.
Reality You pay in muscle. A school lesson from Alaska's Department of Education on a hand-spun generator puts it plainly: whenever you connect the bulb, it suddenly gets harder to crank the generator, and when you disconnect it, it gets easier. Physics calls this Lenz's law: the induced current makes a magnetic field that opposes the change which produced it. A generator does not create energy; it converts the work you put in.
Myth When a prime minister asked what use his discovery was, Faraday replied, “Someday you can tax it.”
Reality A lovely line with no evidence behind it. The fact-checkers at Snopes found it in no account by Faraday or his contemporaries; it only popped up well after his death. William Gladstone, the usual prime minister in the story, did not become prime minister until the year after Faraday died. In 1946 the historian I. Bernard Cohen noted in Nature that the tale appears in various forms, alongside a twin in which Faraday answers, “What good is a new-born baby?”

Wait, really? You can feel the electrons. Crank a small generator with a bulb attached and the extra effort you sense is the current fighting its way through the thin filament. The Alaska lesson goes as far as to say that, in a very real way, you can feel the electrons in the light bulb filament. It also has you spin the generator with its two wires joined directly together, with no bulb at all, and feel what changes.

title: Power from Water, Wind and Sun
description: Watts and watt-hours, water wheels to micro-hydro, wind and solar cells, and what each really gives
tryIt: Read the power labels on five things at home, from a phone charger to a kettle, and rank them against a 350-watt elite cyclist.

concepts.title: How it works: watts, wheels and windmills
concepts.contentHtml:
You have a dynamo now, but cranking it all night is no life. Outside, a stream tumbles down the hillside, the wind hums over the ridge and the sun comes up every morning. Each is a free arm to turn your generator, or in the sun's case, a way to skip the generator altogether.

First, the currency. Power is measured in watts, named after the steam-engine pioneer James Watt; a kilowatt is 1,000 watts. Power is voltage times current, so a 12-volt lamp drawing 2 amps uses 24 watts. Energy over time is counted in watt-hours: run a 40-watt bulb for five hours and you have used 200 watt-hours. Watts say how hard a source pushes at any moment; watt-hours say how much it has delivered by the end of the day.

Water came first. The Greeks used water wheels to grind wheat into flour more than 2,000 years ago, and in 1880 a dynamo driven by a water turbine powered a theatre and storefront in Grand Rapids, Michigan; in 1881 another lit street lights in Niagara Falls. Wind is older still: people sailed boats along the Nile with it as early as 5,000 BC, by 200 BC windmills with woven-reed blades ground grain in Persia and the Middle East, and in the late 1800s and early 1900s small wind-electric generators were widely used.

Sunlight needs no moving parts at all. On 25 April 1954 Daryl Chapin, Calvin Fuller and Gerald Pearson of Bell Labs demonstrated the first practical photovoltaic solar cell, turning sunlight into useful power at about six per cent efficiency. A single cell is small, typically producing about 1 or 2 watts, so cells are wired in chains to make panels.

concepts.title: In the field: how many watts can you get?
concepts.contentHtml:
Before you build anything, do the sums. Off-grid power is a budget: what you can harvest against what you need, with batteries to cover the gaps.

  1. List your needs. Read the watt labels, add up what you would run at once, then multiply by the hours for watt-hours.
  2. Measure the stream. Its power depends on the flow (cubic metres a second), the head (the height the water falls) and gravity. Natural Resources Canada gives power in kilowatts as flow × head × 9.8 × an efficiency of 0.5 to 0.7.
  3. Run the numbers. Their example: 10 metres of head and 0.3 cubic metres a second gives about 15 kW. A garden-sized stream of 10 litres a second falling 2 metres gives 0.01 × 2 × 9.8 × 0.5, about 0.1 kW: a hundred watts.
  4. Check the wind. Small turbines want a site whose annual average wind speed is at least 4 metres a second. A small turbine that can power a single home may be rated at 10 kW, but it only gives that in a strong wind.
  5. Face the sun. Sunlight is strongest at solar noon on clear days; latitude, weather and shade from trees, buildings and hills all cut it.
  6. Plan for the gaps. Hydro runs day and night; wind and sun come and go, so you will need storage.
Safety Water and electricity are a bad mix: the HSE notes that electrical risks are greatest in wet surroundings and outdoors, exactly where wheels and turbines live, so keep everything you build at battery voltage. Never reach into a turning wheel or climb a turbine mast. And the law has a say: in Canada it is illegal to take surface water from a stream without a water licence or other approval, and rules elsewhere vary, so check before you dam or divert anything.

concepts.title: Myth check: cloudy days and free houses
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth Solar panels do nothing on a cloudy day.
Reality Cloud dims the light; it does not switch it off. Flat photovoltaic panels can use global solar radiation, which includes scattered (diffuse) light as well as the direct beam, so they keep working under cloud at lower output. Clouds, dust and pollution all cut how much sunshine reaches the surface.
Myth Any stream or windy hill can run a whole house.
Reality Do the sums from the last card. A garden stream gives perhaps a hundred watts, and an elite cyclist produces about 5 watts for every kilogram of body weight for an hour: a 70 kg rider holding 350 watts is elite. Micro-hydro systems come as small as 0.1 kW for battery-based setups and up to 100 kW, and the site's head and flow, not your wishes, set the limit.

Wait, really? In wind power, size is everything: the length of the blades is the biggest factor in how much electricity a turbine can generate. The largest operating turbines are rated at about 15,000 kilowatts each, so one machine matches a thousand of the 15 kW micro-hydro plants in the Canadian example.

title: Storing Power, Staying Alive
description: Batteries old and new, safe 12-volt lighting, why mains kills, and the shock myths that hurt people
tryIt: Make a pocket lamp by pinching a coin cell between the two legs of an LED (flip it if it stays dark), then lock all spare coin cells well away from children.

concepts.title: How it works: storing charge, and why mains kills
concepts.contentHtml:
The stream freezes at night, the wind drops at dusk and the sun sets on schedule. To have light when nature stops turning your generator you must bottle the electricity, and you must learn exactly how it can kill you.

A battery stores energy as chemistry and gives it back as current. In 1859 the French physicist Gaston Planté invented the lead-acid battery, the first battery that could be recharged: push current back in and its chemistry runs in reverse. Its descendants sit in almost every car, motorcycle and wagon on the road. The light lithium-ion battery came much later. John Goodenough showed in 1980 that a cobalt oxide cathode could give as much as four volts, Akira Yoshino built the first commercially viable lithium-ion battery in 1985, and with Stanley Whittingham they shared the 2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

Now the danger. What harms you is current through your body, and it takes astonishingly little. In OSHA's table for one second of current from hand to foot, a thousandth of an amp (1 milliamp) is a faint tingle; 9 to 30 milliamps is the range where a man cannot let go; 50 to 150 milliamps can stop your breathing and may kill; and from about 1 amp the heart's pumping stops. How much current flows depends on the voltage pushing it and the resistance of the path. Dry skin has a fairly high resistance, but wet skin acts as a conductor. Most batteries carry little risk of electric shock; normal mains voltage, 230 volts in Britain, can kill.

concepts.title: In the field: safe low-voltage light
concepts.contentHtml:
The safest system is one that cannot push a lethal current at all. The HSE's advice for workplaces is to limit the supply voltage to the lowest needed to get the job done: temporary lighting can run at 12, 25, 50 or 110 volts, and battery-operated tools are safest. Build your lights at 12 volts and you keep most of the benefit with little of the danger.

  1. Use LEDs. They make light up to 90% more efficiently than incandescent bulbs, which release 90% of their energy as heat.
  2. Fuse it. Put a fuse first in line from the battery's positive terminal. Fuses melt when too much current flows, protecting the wires from overheating.
  3. Strip off metal. No rings, watches or chains, and use tools with insulated handles; keep loose tools off the battery.
  4. Charge with air and no flames. Charging makes hydrogen and oxygen, and a spark, flame or cigarette can set them off. Charge in a well-ventilated place and stop when it is full.
  5. Connect in order. Take off the earthed terminal (usually the negative) first and put it back last.
  6. Guard your eyes. Wear goggles or a visor whenever you handle batteries.
Safety If someone is stuck to a live household supply, shout for someone to call 999 or 112, and do not touch them. Turn off the source of electricity, or stand on something dry and insulating, such as a plastic mat or wooden box, and push their limb away with a wooden broom handle. If a power line is down, stay at least 6 metres away. Button batteries are a hidden killer: swallowed, one can burn a child's food pipe in just two hours, so get emergency help at once and do not wait for symptoms. Never work on mains wiring.

concepts.title: Myth check: volts, amps and rubber soles
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth It's the volts that kill (or its twin: it's the amps, not the volts).
Reality Both halves matter. The damage is done by current, but the current depends on the voltage and the resistance of the path it follows through the body. A car battery can drive a huge current through a dropped spanner and make it very hot very quickly, yet carries little risk of electric shock, because 12 volts cannot push much current through dry skin. Mains voltage can. And OSHA warns that low voltage does not imply low hazard: longer exposures at even relatively low voltages can be just as dangerous as short exposures at higher ones.
Myth Rubber-soled shoes keep you safe.
Reality Insulation protects only when it is made and rated for the job. OSHA's rule is that insulation must be suitable for the voltage used and conditions such as moisture, and small amounts of impurities in water can turn insulators into conductors. Shoes also do nothing if your body joins both wires of a circuit, hand to hand. HyperPhysics notes that insulating shoes can help you escape serious shock if one hand touches a 120-volt circuit, which is why engineers keep one hand in a pocket: a habit, not a licence.

Wait, really? A bird can sit on a high-voltage wire without harm, since both of its feet are at the same voltage. And someone struck by lightning does not stay electrified: the human body does not store electricity, so it is perfectly safe to touch a lightning victim to give first aid. Someone still touching a live wire is another matter entirely.
